summary: Astronaut Health Monitor is a proactive AI that watches five simulated data streams for each astronaut (suit vitals, urine chemistry, habitat air, radiation, and face-camera fatigue signals). It detects 20 health and safety conditions, from hypoxia and cabin CO2 buildup to dehydration and solar particle events. Using an explainable machine-learning ensemble, hard safety rules, sensor-fault checks and trend-based early warning, it raises graded alerts with the likely cause, the readings behind it, and a recommended action. On 420 unseen simulated test rows it reached 86.7% accuracy and missed none of the 400 problem cases. All data is simulated and AI-assisted, and thresholds are placeholders, so this is a research prototype, not a medical device.
details:
ASTRONAUT HEALTH MONITOR
A proactive AI that detects health and safety problems early, explains them, and recommends what to do

THE PROBLEM

On missions to the Moon and Mars, crews will be days or months from medical help, and messages to Earth will be delayed. Problems that are easy to fix when caught early, such as rising cabin CO2, dehydration, a failing suit scrubber or a solar particle event, can become dangerous when noticed late. Many risks do not show up in a single sensor. Tiredness, for example, appears as a mix of slower blinking, more yawning, falling heart rate variability and rising CO2. Crews need a system that watches many signals at once, notices trends before limits are crossed, and tells them clearly what it sees and why.

OUR SOLUTION

Astronaut Health Monitor is a proactive monitoring AI built around classical machine learning. It reads five streams of simulated data for each astronaut, predicts which of 20 health or safety conditions is developing, and raises graded alerts (watch, caution, warning, critical). Each alert includes the most likely condition, a confidence level, the readings that drove the decision, and a recommended action. The system is designed to speak up early: it tracks how the probability of “normal” falls over time and can flag a developing problem before any hard limit is crossed.

WHAT MAKES IT DIFFERENT

Most monitors compare one sensor to one limit. This system combines signals: it reads breathing, CO2 and facial signs together to separate fatigue from CO2 exposure, and urine chemistry together with heart rate to separate dehydration from heat stress. It is proactive, using trends and a falling normal-probability to alert before a limit is crossed. It is layered for safety, with hard rules, model predictions, anomaly checks and sensor-fault checks working together. And it is transparent: every alert says what it sees, why, and what to do.

FIVE DATA STREAMS

All data in this project is simulated. No real astronaut data was used.

  • Suit, per astronaut: heart rate, blood oxygen (SpO2), breathing rate, heart rate variability, skin temperature, activity level, suit oxygen and suit CO2.
  • Urine, per astronaut, every simulated two hours: pH, oxalate, volume and specific gravity, which indicate hydration and kidney stone risk.
  • Habitat, shared: CO2, oxygen, pressure, temperature and humidity.
  • Radiation: dose rate, cumulative dose, a solar particle event flag and the shielding zone the astronaut is in.
  • Face camera, per astronaut: eye aspect ratio, blink rate, yawn rate, head tilt and a drowsiness flag, used to detect fatigue, stress and motion sickness.

THE 20 CONDITIONS

Cardiovascular: resting tachycardia, cardiovascular deconditioning, irregular rhythm. Respiratory and air: hypoxia, hypercapnia (cabin CO2 buildup), suit scrubber failure, cabin pressure loss. Thermal and fluids: heat stress, cold stress, dehydration, kidney stone risk. Brain and behaviour: acute fatigue, chronic sleep deprivation, psychological stress, space motion sickness. Radiation: solar particle event exposure, approaching the cumulative dose limit, poor shielding. Physical: overexertion and sedentary deconditioning. A healthy “nominal” class lets the system recognise normal readings at every activity level.

HOW IT WORKS

  1. Data. We generated about 150 examples per condition with AI assistance, then cleaned and validated them, removing malformed rows, impossible values and duplicates. This gave about 3,200 rows. Each example is a snapshot of one astronaut that includes short-term trends, such as how fast heart rate or SpO2 is changing.
  2. Context-aware features. A heart rate of 140 is normal during exercise and alarming at rest, so the model works with deviations from what is expected for the astronaut’s current activity. We also derive scores for hydration stress, kidney stone risk, fatigue, stress, respiratory load, heat load, and effective radiation dose given the shielding zone.
  3. Ensemble model. Four models vote: gradient boosting, random forest, extra trees and logistic regression. Probabilities are calibrated so that confidence values are more meaningful.
  4. Safety layer. Hard rules for critical limits, such as very low SpO2, high CO2, low pressure or a solar event in an exposed zone, fire immediately and do not depend on the model. Life-critical thresholds should never rest on a learned model alone.
  5. Reliability checks. The system flags sensor problems (impossible values and flat-lined sensors) and uses an anomaly detector to warn when a reading matches none of the known conditions.
  6. Alert logic. Alerts require the same prediction on consecutive readings, which prevents flickering. An early-warning flag appears when the probability of “normal” keeps falling.
  7. Explanations. Every alert lists the readings that deviate most from normal, plus a recommended action.

We chose classical machine learning deliberately. It trains in under a minute on a laptop, runs on modest hardware without a GPU (important for spacecraft computers), and is easier to inspect and explain than a large language model.

TESTING AND RESULTS

We tested the system in two ways. Cross-validation, where entire blocks of similar rows are held out, gave about 98.8% accuracy. This number is optimistic, because all the data comes from one generation process. The more meaningful test used a separate set of 420 unseen simulated rows (20 per condition), generated independently. On it the system reached 86.7% accuracy and classified none of the 400 problem rows as healthy. In a safety setting, missing a real problem is the worst failure, so this is the figure we care about most.

The test also showed weaknesses. Most errors came from conditions that look alike, such as cardiovascular deconditioning versus sedentary deconditioning. Healthy readings at higher activity were sometimes flagged as problems (9 of 20 healthy test rows in our first test). We plan to add more healthy examples and to measure how much the persistence rule reduces these false alarms. We report these results as they are, because they show where the system needs to improve.

WHAT WE TRIED FIRST

We first tried fine-tuning a Qwen language model with LoRA on 2,400 examples. Training failed with a GPU out-of-memory error on the free hardware available to us, so it produced no usable model. We kept the attempt in our Drive folder, labelled as an experiment, and switched to the classical approach, which turned out to be faster, lighter and more explainable.

CURRENT STATUS

Working and verified: the trained model, the alert engine (rules, sensor-fault checks, anomaly detection, persistence and early warning), and the evaluation on unseen data. The public demo page replays recorded outputs of the trained model on unseen simulated scenarios, showing how status and alerts evolve as problems develop. Prototype code for a live API, a data simulator and the dashboard is in the repository, but a fully connected live deployment is still future work, and we describe it that way.

LIMITATIONS AND RESPONSIBLE USE

This is a research prototype, not a medical device. All data is simulated and was generated with AI assistance, so the accuracy numbers show how the system behaves on our simulated scenarios, not how it would perform on real astronauts. Thresholds and recommended actions are placeholders that must be replaced with values from NASA standards and reviewed by flight surgeons. A real system would also need a personal baseline for each astronaut, because normal heart rate and HRV differ between people. The system is meant to support human decisions, never replace them, so every alert shows its reasons and leaves the decision to the crew and medical team.

AI USE DISCLOSURE

We used AI tools (Google Gemini and Anthropic’s Claude) to help generate synthetic training examples and to write and debug code. Our team defined the problem and the 20 conditions, chose the approach, ran the experiments, evaluated the results and made the design decisions.

NEXT STEPS

  • Validate against public NASA datasets, such as those in the NASA Open Science Data Repository, and real physiological recordings.
  • Replace placeholder thresholds with clinician-reviewed limits.
  • Learn a personal baseline per astronaut and add longer-term trend models.
  • Connect real sensors and live camera analysis, processed on the device to protect privacy.
  • Reduce false alarms and separate look-alike conditions with richer signals, such as heart rate variability over time.
  • Deploy the live backend and dashboard.

WHY IT MATTERS

Autonomy will be essential for deep-space missions. A monitoring system that is explainable, runs on modest hardware and is honest about its uncertainty could help crews catch problems early and decide what to do when Earth cannot answer in time.
